title: How would you estimate how many passengers use Heathrow on an average day?
description: A step-by-step estimate for "How many passengers fly from or to Heathrow on an average day?" with the approach, the maths and a sanity check.
hook: Heathrow handles roughly 230,000 passengers on an average day: about 1,300 take-offs and landings, each with an average of about 225 seats, 80% full. The real figure for 2025 was about 231,000 a day, and the step that gets you there is accounting for big long-haul jets rather than assuming every plane is a short-haul one. Have a go yourself before reading on.
body:
The question

How many passengers fly from or to Heathrow on an average day?

Pin down the unit before any numbers. Airports count passenger movements: every arrival and every departure. A traveller changing planes at Heathrow lands and then takes off again, so they count twice even though they are one person. Ask which the interviewer wants:

"I'll estimate passenger movements, arrivals plus departures, on an average day, which is how airports report traffic. I can convert to unique travellers at the end if useful."

The approach: start from flights, not people

Estimating from London's population would be hopeless: Heathrow serves visitors, connecting passengers and people from across the country. The airport side is far easier to reason about, because runway capacity limits it. So size it from the supply side:

Flights a day × average seats per flight × share of seats filled (the load factor).

Choosing the side that is easier to estimate is a skill in itself; see whether to size from buyers or sellers.

Step by step

1. Flights a day: 1,300

Heathrow has two runways in constant use. Assume each handles roughly 37 movements an hour over about 17.5 operating hours (there are restrictions at night): 2 × 37 × 17.5 = about 1,300 take-offs and landings a day.

2. Average seats: 225

This is where most candidates go wrong. Heathrow is a long-haul hub, so a big share of its flights are wide-body jets.

Flight typeShare of flightsSeatsContribution
Short-haul (Europe, domestic)55%18099
Long-haul (wide-body)45%280126
Weighted average100%225

3. Load factor: 80%

Airlines at a busy hub fill most seats. 225 × 80% = 180 passengers per flight.

4. The answer

1,300 × 180 = about 234,000 passenger movements a day.

Check against the real figure

Heathrow reported 84.5M passengers and about 478,000 air transport movements in 2025 (Heathrow media centre). That is about 231,000 passengers and 1,309 movements a day, or roughly 177 passengers per movement. Our estimate is within about 1%.

The useful comparison is with the shortcut many candidates use: 1,300 flights × 180 seats × 80% = 187,000. The flight count is right; the error is entirely in seats per flight. Assuming every aircraft is short-haul ignores that long-haul jets carry more than half of the passengers in our mix (126 of the 225 average seats).

Sanity check from a second angle

Turn the answer back into something you can picture. 234,000 movements a day means about 117,000 departing passengers, or roughly 6,700 an hour over 17.5 hours. Spread across several terminals, that is a few thousand people an hour in each, which fits a very busy airport. If you had got 2 million a day, the security queues alone would tell you something was wrong.

What a strong answer sounds like

"I estimate about 230,000 passenger movements a day: 1,300 flights, about 225 seats each because nearly half are long-haul wide-bodies, and 80% full. The seat mix is the swing factor; with all short-haul jets I'd get 187,000. Connecting passengers count twice, so the number of unique travellers is lower."

A weak answer says "London has 9 million people, maybe 2% fly each day" and has no way to check itself.

Common mistakes

  • One aircraft size. At a long-haul hub, the mix of aircraft drives the answer. Segment it.
  • Mixing units. Movements, departures and unique travellers are different numbers. Name the one you are sizing.
  • Forgetting the load factor. Seats are not passengers.
  • Treating the average as typical. Heathrow's busiest day in 2025, 1 August, passed 270,000 passengers, about 17% above the average. Capacity planning needs the peak.

Practise it

1. Suppose a quarter of passenger movements are by connecting travellers. How many unique people use Heathrow a day?

Show the answer

Non-connecting: 75% × 234,000 = 175,500 people. Connecting: 25% × 234,000 = 58,500 movements, but each person makes two, so 29,250 people. Total: about 205,000 unique travellers. (The 25% is illustrative; check the real share before using it.)

2. Load factor drops to 75%. What is the new daily figure?

Show the answer

225 × 75% = 168.75 passengers per flight × 1,300 = about 219,000. Five points of load factor is worth about 15,000 passengers a day.

3. The airport earns an illustrative $45 in charges per departing passenger. What is that worth a year?

Show the answer

Departing passengers: 234,000 ÷ 2 = 117,000 a day × $45 = about $5.3M a day. × 365 = about $1.9B a year.

Where to practise next
